predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, only about nine months have passed since the February 21, 2025 episode, while the prediction is explicitly about the *medium to long term*, so it is too early to judge definitively.

There is **supportive directional evidence**:
- Large institutions and asset managers (e.g., DWS) now explicitly describe stablecoins as *emerging core payment infrastructure*, noting that stablecoin transaction volumes already rival or surpass card networks like Visa and Mastercard in raw on‑chain volume, even if much of that is still crypto‑native activity. ([coindesk.com](https://www.coindesk.com/markets/2025/10/14/dws-sees-stablecoins-emerging-as-core-payments-infrastructure?utm_source=openai))  
- Reports from Keyrock/Bitso project stablecoin payment volumes exceeding **$1T annually by 2030**, driven by institutional, FX, and cross‑border flows, implying they may become a major rail in global payments. ([coindesk.com](https://www.coindesk.com/markets/2025/08/14/stablecoin-payments-projected-to-top-usd1t-annually-by-2030-market-maker-keyrock-says?utm_source=openai))  
- Analyses suggest stablecoins could handle **5–10% of global payments by 2030**, and that by late 2025 roughly **3% of the world’s $200T in cross‑border payments** already move via stablecoins. ([coindesk.com](https://www.coindesk.com/sponsored-content/building-the-infrastructure-for-the-usd2-trillion-stablecoin-economy?utm_source=openai))  
- Major consumer/payment platforms (Stripe, PayPal, and now Klarna) are integrating or launching stablecoins and using them as underlying rails while keeping existing consumer-facing experiences, which matches the *“built upon and substantially leverage these things”* part of the prediction. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/roomykhan/2025/11/16/stablecoins-and-blockchain-becoming-the-backbone-of-finance/?utm_source=openai))

However, **the strong version of the claim has not been met yet**:
- Stablecoins, while rapidly growing, still account for **well under 10% of global payments** and less than 1% of all daily transfer volume, so they are *not yet* the “common rail” for most payments. ([coindesk.com](https://www.coindesk.com/sponsored-content/building-the-infrastructure-for-the-usd2-trillion-stablecoin-economy?utm_source=openai))  
- Traditional card networks and bank rails remain dominant in consumer payments, and it is impossible at this early stage to verify that *“most consumer‑facing payment networks”* will ultimately be built on top of stablecoins.

Because the key outcomes are framed over a medium‑to‑long‑term horizon (years, not months) and current data shows only an early trend rather than a completed shift, the prediction cannot reasonably be called right or wrong yet, so **"inconclusive" (too early)** is the appropriate classification.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction was about *sequence* and *relative strength* of adoption: (1) stablecoins would first gain traction in international/cross‑border B2B use cases, and (2) domestic B2B payments in places like the U.S. would follow only after those cross‑border rails were established.

By late 2025, available data and industry surveys show that cross‑border B2B is indeed the leading and earliest mainstream use case for stablecoins, while domestic B2B usage exists but is still secondary:

- Fireblocks’ 2025 industry report notes that domestic payment systems in many regions already offer instant settlement, whereas international flows remain constrained by legacy correspondent banking; as a result, **cross-border payments are explicitly described as the main driver of stablecoin adoption, especially for high‑volume B2B flows**, and banks are reported to be *twice as likely* to prioritize cross‑border stablecoin use over other use cases. ([fireblocks.com](https://fireblocks.com/report/state-of-stablecoins/?utm_source=openai))
- A bank survey summarized by Grant Thornton/Fireblocks finds **58% of traditional banks already use stablecoins for cross‑border payments**, versus just **9% for B2B invoicing and 9% for merchant settlement**, indicating that cross‑border B2B usage is far more established than domestic B2B applications. ([grantthornton.com.cy](https://www.grantthornton.com.cy/insights/Distributedledgertechnology/Stablecoins-Promise-Peril-and-the-Policy-Race/?utm_source=openai))
- Broader market analysis similarly frames business use of stablecoins as concentrated in **paying suppliers and contractors, especially across borders**, and highlights rapidly growing cross‑border stablecoin flows in key corridors (e.g., U.S.–Mexico, Europe–Africa). ([cointeeth.com](https://www.cointeeth.com/news/regulatory-trilogy-is-a-new-era-for-stablecoins?utm_source=openai))  A dedicated Artemis/Castle Island study on B2B stablecoin payments reports a 30x increase to over $3 billion in monthly B2B stablecoin volume by 2025, characterizing this growth specifically in terms of **global, cross‑border business payments**. ([prnewswire.com](https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/b2b-stablecoin-payments-surge-30x-to-3-billion-monthly-volume-in-2025-302487975.html?utm_source=openai))

At the same time, evidence shows that *domestic* B2B usage in advanced markets like the U.S. is materializing, but later and at smaller scale, consistent with the prediction:

- Stripe only began supporting **USDC acceptance for U.S. merchants in October 2024**, with usage then spreading globally; this enables on‑chain payments (including purely domestic U.S. commerce) but comes after years of stablecoin use in trading and cross‑border flows. ([forbes.com](https://www.forbes.com/sites/roomykhan/2025/11/16/stablecoins-and-blockchain-becoming-the-backbone-of-finance/?utm_source=openai))
- In 2025, PayPal rolled out “Pay with Crypto” for **U.S. merchants**, allowing them to accept payments in crypto including stablecoins like USDC and to hold balances in PYUSD—again, a domestic merchant/B2B capability deployed after cross‑border and remittance use cases were already well‑established. ([jdsupra.com](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/the-payments-newsletter-including-7159979/?utm_source=openai))
- The same bank survey showing 58% cross‑border usage but only 9% in merchant settlement and 9% in B2B invoicing implies domestic B2B/payables use is **present but lags significantly** behind cross‑border adoption rather than leading it. ([grantthornton.com.cy](https://www.grantthornton.com.cy/insights/Distributedledgertechnology/Stablecoins-Promise-Peril-and-the-Policy-Race/?utm_source=openai))

Taken together, the empirical pattern as of November 2025 is that (a) cross‑border B2B and remittance flows clearly led the way in real‑world stablecoin adoption, and (b) domestic B2B and merchant payments—particularly in the U.S.—are arriving later and remain smaller but are now emerging. That matches both elements of the prediction, so it is best characterized as **right**.

The prediction is about **"the coming years"** (a multi‑year horizon) and claims that:

1. U.S. labor productivity will **continue to increase**.
2. The **rate of productivity growth** will be **further boosted by AI and related software tools**.

As of **November 30, 2025**, less than one year has passed since the prediction (February 21, 2025). That is far too short to evaluate a multi‑year trend or to reliably attribute any observed productivity changes specifically to AI and new software tools, as opposed to business cycles, capital investment, or measurement issues. Productivity trends are typically assessed over several years.

Preliminary data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics show that nonfarm business labor productivity has indeed risen over the last decade and has shown some recent quarters of strong growth, but economists are still debating the permanence of this uptick and the extent to which AI is the driver. These early signals are not enough to declare that a durable, AI‑driven acceleration in productivity growth has been established.

Because the **timeframe the predictor specified (“coming years”) has not yet elapsed** and any causal impact of AI on trend productivity growth cannot yet be robustly established, the correct classification is **“inconclusive (too early)”**.

Available evidence as of **30 Nov 2025** shows:

1. **Arc’s financial position today**  
   Arc launched in 2021 with more than **$650M in philanthropic funding**, described in public materials as an endowment-scale pool intended to fully sustain its scientists for renewable eight‑year terms, with additional fundraising since then. This is philanthropic capital, not proceeds from commercial spinouts. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_Institute?utm_source=openai))  

2. **Spinout activity so far**  
   Arc’s model explicitly includes future for‑profit spinouts via its Translational Program, but its own materials and independent coverage focus on scientific tools (e.g., bridge RNA genome editing, the Evo DNA foundation model) rather than on mature commercial products or exits. ([arcinstitute.org](https://arcinstitute.org/model?utm_source=openai))  
   
   The clearest example of an Arc‑connected biotech startup is **Stylus Medicine**, which emerged from stealth in 2025 with an $85M Series A; its scientific foundation comes from academic founders including Arc co‑founder Patrick Hsu. This is an early‑stage therapeutics company with no approved drugs, revenues, or exit on anything like *Moderna* or *Ozempic* scale. ([app.dealroom.co](https://app.dealroom.co/companies/stylus_medicine?utm_source=openai))  

3. **No Moderna/Ozempic‑scale outcome yet**  
   Broad searches for Arc‑related spinouts, IPOs, acquisitions, or approved blockbuster drugs find **no evidence** that any Arc‑originated company has yet achieved a market cap, product revenue, or exit comparable to Moderna or Ozempic by late 2025. Coverage of Arc remains about research breakthroughs and partnerships (e.g., Nvidia) rather than monetization or massive liquidity events. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arc_Institute?utm_source=openai))  

Because the prediction is explicitly **conditional and long‑term** — *if* a spinout reaches Moderna/Ozempic‑level success, *then* its returns could endow Arc and make it self‑sustaining — the relevant antecedent (a blockbuster Arc spinout) **has not occurred yet**, and realistically could take a decade or more to materialize.

So we **cannot** assess whether the claimed financial consequence would follow; we can only say that the condition has not yet been met. Given the long time horizon and the absence of a qualifying spinout so far, the status of this prediction is **“too early to tell.”

predictions.explanation:
The asteroid in question is 2024 YR4, an Apollo‑type near‑Earth object whose orbit crosses Earth’s and which has a possible close approach on 22 December 2032.

• Around 19–20 February 2025, NASA’s Center for Near‑Earth Object Studies (via Sentry) and ESA indeed reported that 2024 YR4 had an impact probability of about 1.5% for 2032, with an estimated size roughly 40–90 m (≈130–300 ft) across. Multiple outlets summarized this as a 1.5% chance of impact after a peak of about 3.1%, matching Friedberg’s “~1.5%” description tied explicitly to the then‑current trajectory estimates. ([snopes.com](https://www.snopes.com/news/2025/02/21/nasa-asteroid-hitting-earth-2032/?utm_source=openai))

• Within days, new observations rapidly drove the modeled impact probability down: Sky at Night and other sources note that the chance fell from 3.1% to 1.5% on 19 Feb, to 0.28% on 20 Feb, and then to about 0.005% by 23 Feb 2025. ([skyatnightmagazine.com](https://www.skyatnightmagazine.com/space-science/asteroid-2024-yr4?utm_source=openai)) Subsequently, NASA and ESA further reduced the risk to roughly 0.001–0.004%, effectively zero, and the object was downgraded to Torino Scale 0. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/cce39c01ab94ac1edae00024dc35169c?utm_source=openai))

• Energy‑yield estimates from NASA‑linked analyses and expert commentary put a 40–90 m stony asteroid like 2024 YR4 in the rough range of ~7–10 megatons of TNT if it actually hit Earth—enough for severe city‑scale damage but not a global catastrophe. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_YR4?utm_source=openai)) Friedberg’s “up to ~20 megatons if it’s near 300 feet” is a back‑of‑the‑envelope extrapolation from the upper end of the size range and cannot be directly validated or falsified without an actual impact.

• Crucially, the core of his statement is a probabilistic forecast about *whether* the asteroid will hit Earth in 2032 and, if so, the chance of human casualties. As of 30 November 2025, 2032 is still in the future, and 2024 YR4 has obviously not impacted Earth yet. The updated orbital solutions now imply an extremely small impact probability, but whether the true physical outcome in 2032 is “no impact” (which would mean the real ex ante probability was effectively near zero) cannot be definitively judged until after that date.

Because the underlying event (any 2032 impact and associated loss of life) has not yet occurred, the correctness of Friedberg’s *forecasted* 1.5% impact chance and ~15% conditional fatality chance cannot be empirically evaluated. His descriptive claim about the then‑current NASA estimate (~1.5%) was accurate, but the predictive content about the actual 2032 outcome remains untestable at this time. Hence the status is **inconclusive (too early to tell)**.

- A tweet (archived via TwiCopy) from the official **This Week in Startups** account recaps **“The All-In Podcast LIVE @ SXSW”**, explicitly naming **@jason, Chamath Palihapitiya, and david friedberg** on stage with guests Bryan Johnson, Colin & Samir, and Chris Williamson, and mentions a “room full of fans,” corroborating that the live SXSW-affiliated show with Jason and Friedberg did in fact occur and drew a sizable audience. ([twicopy.com](https://twicopy.com/twistartups/tweet/1900366709992939596?utm_source=openai))

We do not have direct documentation confirming the **$30 application fee via allin.com/events**, but the main factual components Jason predicted—**being in Austin for SXSW on March 13, Jason and Friedberg co-hosting live interviews focused on media/business, and an intimate event with food and drinks for a few hundred people—are all borne out by the available sources.** Therefore, the prediction is best classified as **right**.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction explicitly concerns a *“post‑AI era”* over the coming **decades**, in which AI allegedly makes routine things like:

- Deep mining toward the Earth’s interior ("500 miles down") for rare earth minerals
- Large‑scale space projects such as **colonizing the Moon**

As of **November 30, 2025**, none of this has occurred:

- Current mining operations are limited to relatively shallow depths in the Earth’s crust; there is no technology or active industrial practice approaching hundreds of miles deep extraction for rare earths or anything else.
- Human activity on the Moon is limited to robotic missions and planning for future crewed missions (e.g., NASA’s Artemis program and various commercial lunar initiatives). There is **no permanent lunar colony or routine colonization activity** in operation yet.
- AI has advanced rapidly and is being used in engineering, logistics, and scientific research, but it has not yet demonstrably enabled the kind of massive, routine, planetary‑scale and space‑colonization projects described.

Because the prediction’s implied time horizon is *“the post‑AI era” over the coming decades*, and we are only in **2025**, it is **too early to determine** whether AI will in fact unlock the level of routine deep‑Earth mining and Moon colonization described. The relevant future period has not arrived, and the prediction is not framed to be testable this soon.

Therefore, the status of the prediction is **inconclusive (too early to tell)** given the current date.
predictions.grok_explanation: The prediction is for the 'post-AI era' (coming decades), where AI enables routine ultra-deep mining (e.g., 500 miles/~800 km for rare earths) and Moon colonization. As of Dec 2025 (~10 months post-podcast), deepest borehole remains Kola Superdeep at 12.2 km ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kola_Superdeep_Borehole)); deepest mine ~4 km (Mponeng Gold, [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_deepest_mines)). China's 10.9 km well in Feb 2025 ([SCIO](http://english.scio.gov.cn/m/chinavoices/2025-02/21/content_117725400.html)) far short. Moon: Artemis II flyby 2025, landing 2026, no colonization ([NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/feature/artemis/)). AI aids mining efficiency ([Omdena](https://www.omdena.com/blog/top-24-global-mining-companies-driving-ai-transformation-in-2025)) but not these feats. Too early for long-term prediction.

predictions.explanation:
Jason makes the prediction near the end of the Feb. 21, 2025 episode *“The Stablecoin Future, Milei's Memecoin, DOGE for the DoD, Grok 3, Why Stripe Stays Private,”* saying about Friedberg’s upcoming Celebrity Jeopardy! appearance: **“We are going to do a recap of every single question.”** ([happyscribe.com](https://www.happyscribe.com/public/all-in-with-chamath-jason-sacks-friedberg/the-stablecoin-future-milei-s-memecoin-doge-for-the-dod-grok-3-why-stripe-stays-private?utm_source=openai))  

Friedberg’s Celebrity Jeopardy! episode then airs the following week (ABC’s Celebrity Jeopardy! for Wednesday, Feb. 26, 2025, discussed in Jeopardy forums and coverage of that game with Ana Navarro and David Friedberg). ([reddit.com](https://www.reddit.com//r/Jeopardy/comments/1iz3cew?utm_source=openai))  

After it airs, the All-In hosts do return to the topic in the Mar. 1, 2025 episode *“Epstein Files Flop, State of the Market, Autonomous Robots, Trump's Gold Card, Friedberg on Jeopardy,”* which has a segment explicitly titled **“Friedberg recaps his experience on Celebrity Jeopardy!”** from 4:40–14:22. ([podscripts.co](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/all-in-with-chamath-jason-sacks-friedberg/epstein-files-flop-state-of-the-market-autonomous-robots-trumps-gold-card-friedberg-on-jeopardy))  However, the transcript of that segment shows they:

- Play and react to a few highlight clues (e.g., the African geography Daily Double about Mount Kilimanjaro and the Hoosiers sports-movie Daily Double),
- Talk about his nerves, buzzer timing strategy, preparation, and the charity payout,
- Then move on to the next topic around the 14:22 mark.

They **do not** systematically walk through each clue from the game or attempt a question‑by‑question recap; only a handful of specific questions are mentioned before the conversation shifts to other subjects. ([podscripts.co](https://podscripts.co/podcasts/all-in-with-chamath-jason-sacks-friedberg/epstein-files-flop-state-of-the-market-autonomous-robots-trumps-gold-card-friedberg-on-jeopardy))  

Search across later episode descriptions and transcript indices for the All-In feed shows no separate episode or extended segment where they later go back and cover *every* question from Friedberg’s Jeopardy game—this Mar. 1 recap is the only substantial Jeopardy-focused segment. ([everand.com](https://www.everand.com/podcast/834047929/Epstein-Files-Flop-State-of-the-Market-Autonomous-Robots-Trump-s-Gold-Card-Friedberg-on-Jeopardy-0-00-Bestie-intros-1-41-Epstein-files-first?utm_source=openai))  

Since the follow-up content is a general highlight/experience recap and not a comprehensive, question-by-question rundown of the entire episode, Jason’s prediction that they would **“do a recap of every single question”** did **not** come true.
